hub.lead: Practical, plain-English guides for people starting or growing a small business in Blackpool. They cover the admin, the money and the day-to-day reality of working from a small unit, with links to the official guidance wherever a rule is involved.

sections.html:
Most people who message us about a unit are not property experts. They are makers, repairers, online sellers and tradespeople who have outgrown a spare room or a garage. The questions they ask are rarely about square feet. They want to know whether they will pay business rates, whether they need insurance, how to get on Google Maps, or whether to set up as a sole trader first.

These guides answer those questions in one place. They are written for small, local businesses, not corporations, and they try to be honest about what is simple and what needs proper advice. Where a rule applies, we link to GOV.UK, HSE, HMRC, Companies House or Blackpool Council so you can check the current position yourself.

sections.h2: Getting started and getting set up
sections.html:
If you are at the very beginning, start here. These guides walk through the first decisions and the paperwork that follows.

  • How to start a business in Blackpool: a step-by-step route from idea to first customer, including registering with HMRC and keeping records.
  • Sole trader or limited company: the real differences in paperwork, liability and tax, and why many people start simple.
  • Small business unit ideas: if you are still choosing what to do, see the kinds of businesses that work well from a small unit.

Where you work shapes your costs, your hours and how customers see you. These guides help you weigh up the options and make the most of the space you pick.

  • Moving your business out of home: the signs it is time, the costs to compare and a calm plan for the move itself.
  • Business unit vs shop vs coworking: an honest comparison of the three most common next steps for a small business.
  • How to set up a small workshop: layout, power, storage walls and dust, for anyone making or fixing things.
  • Working in a windowless unit: lighting, air, breaks and the small habits that make an enclosed space comfortable.

These are the topics people worry about most, and the ones where a little knowledge goes a long way. Each guide explains the basics and points you to the official source.

  • Business rates for small units: what rateable value means, how Small Business Rate Relief works and who to ask.
  • Small business insurance guide: the covers small firms commonly consider, and the one that is compulsory once you employ people.
  • Health and safety in a small unit: risk assessments, fire safety, electrics and working alone, scaled to a one or two person business.

A unit is only useful if people can find you. These guides cover being visible online and selling face to face around town.

  • Google Business Profile address guide: how to list a unit address properly so you show up in local searches without breaking Google's rules.
  • Selling at Blackpool markets: how market trading works, what the council licenses and how to store your stall kit between events.
  • Running a seasonal business in Blackpool: planning around the visitor season and the Illuminations, and getting through the quiet months.

Read them in any order. Each one stands on its own, and they link to each other where a topic overlaps. If you only have ten minutes, these three cover the most ground:

  1. Get the structure rightDecide how you will trade and register with HMRC in good time. The sole trader guide explains the choice.
  2. Know your running costsAdd rent, electricity, insurance and any business rates together before you commit to premises. The rates guide explains what to ask.
  3. Make yourself findableOnce you have an address, set up your Google Business Profile properly so local customers can find you.

The guides are general. They will not replace an accountant, an insurance broker or a solicitor when your situation is unusual, but they should help you ask those people better questions.

pages.title: How to Start a Business in Blackpool | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: A practical step-by-step guide to starting a small business in Blackpool: testing your idea, registering with HMRC, records, money and premises.
pages.lead: Starting a business is mostly a series of small, sensible decisions made in the right order. This guide takes you from a rough idea to your first paying customer, with links to the official rules at each step.

sections.h2: Test the idea before you spend money
sections.html:
The cheapest stage of any business is the one before you commit to costs. Use it well. Write down, in a sentence, who you are selling to and why they would choose you. If you cannot do that yet, keep talking to potential customers until you can.

Then test it in the smallest way you can. Sell a handful of items online. Take a table at a craft fair. Do three jobs for friends of friends at a fair price and ask for honest feedback. You are looking for proof that people will pay, not just that they like the idea.

  • Work out your price per item or per hour, including materials and travel.
  • Check what similar businesses on the Fylde coast charge.
  • Note how long each sale or job really takes you.

Blackpool has a strong visitor economy as well as a local resident market, so ask yourself which one you are serving. The answer changes when you will be busy and how you will find customers.

Most new small businesses start as a sole trader or set up a limited company. A sole trader is the simplest: you and the business are legally the same, and you pay income tax on your profits through Self Assessment. A limited company is a separate legal entity registered with Companies House, with more paperwork and more formal duties.

There is no single right answer. Our guide to choosing between sole trader and limited company sets out the practical differences. If you are going into business with someone else, a partnership is another option, and GOV.UK explains each structure.

sections.h2: Register with HMRC at the right time
sections.html:
If you trade as a sole trader, you need to tell HMRC and register for Self Assessment once you are required to. GOV.UK explains that small amounts of trading income can be covered by the trading allowance, and that you must register if your income goes over it. The deadline to register is 5 October after the end of the tax year in which you started, but registering earlier is easier and means you will not forget.

If you set up a limited company, you register it with Companies House. Since November 2025, directors need to verify their identity with Companies House as part of that process. The company then has its own tax responsibilities, including Corporation Tax.

VAT is separate. You only have to register once your taxable turnover passes the VAT threshold, though some businesses choose to register voluntarily. Check GOV.UK for the current figure rather than relying on what you heard from a friend a few years ago.

sections.h2: Set up simple records and a separate account
sections.html:
Good records save you money and stress at tax time. You do not need complex software to begin, but you do need a system you will actually use.

  1. Open a separate accountKeep business money apart from personal spending. It makes your figures obvious at a glance.
  2. Keep every receiptPhotograph paper receipts the day you get them. Allowable expenses reduce the profit you pay tax on.
  3. Log income as it arrivesDate, customer, amount and what it was for. A spreadsheet is fine at the start.
  4. Put tax asideMove a share of each payment into a savings pot so the tax bill is never a shock.

If you hold customer names, phone numbers or addresses, you are handling personal data. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) explains whether you need to pay the data protection fee, and many small businesses do.

Think about insurance before you start trading, not after something goes wrong. Public liability, product liability and cover for your tools or stock are common for small firms, and employers' liability insurance is a legal requirement once you employ people. Our small business insurance guide explains each one in plain English.

Health and safety applies to the self-employed too, especially if you use tools or have clients visit. Our guide to health and safety in a small unit scales the HSE basics down to a one-person business.

Some activities also need a licence or registration, such as selling food or trading on the street. Blackpool Council's licensing pages list what applies locally.

Many businesses start at the kitchen table, and that is fine. The question is when home stops working. Common signs are stock in every room, tools you cannot use because of noise, or clients you would rather not invite into your house.

When that happens, compare your options honestly. A shop gives you passing trade but usually a longer lease. Coworking gives you a desk but rarely somewhere to keep stock. A small unit gives you space, privacy and access at any hour. Our comparison of units, shops and coworking goes through the trade-offs.

At The Rock Factory, ground-floor units start at 150 sq ft for £65 a week, which is about £282 a month, with lighting, electricity and Wi-Fi already connected and rolling monthly terms. If you are not sure what size you need, the unit comparison page lays them out together.

Early customers usually come from people who already know you, then from people who can find you easily. Cover both.

  • Tell everyone you know what you do, in one clear sentence.
  • Set up a Google Business Profile with a proper address so you appear in local searches.
  • Ask happy customers for a review straight away, while the job is fresh.
  • Try face-to-face selling at Blackpool markets and events if your product suits it.
  • Join local business groups online and offline, and offer help, not just adverts.

This is general information, not legal, tax or financial advice. Registration rules, allowances and thresholds can change, usually from the start of a new tax year. Check the GOV.UK pages listed below for the current rules, and talk to an accountant if your situation is anything other than straightforward.

faqs: Do I need to register a business before I make my first sale?

Not always on day one, but you should check GOV.UK early. Sole traders must register for Self Assessment by 5 October after the tax year they start, if their trading income takes them over the trading allowance. Limited companies must be registered with Companies House before they trade as a company.
Can I start a business while I am still employed?
Yes, many people do. Check your employment contract for anything about outside work, and remember your business profit is taxed alongside your wages through Self Assessment.
Do I need a business bank account as a sole trader?
It is not always a legal requirement for sole traders, but a separate account makes record keeping far easier. Limited companies need their own account because the company is a separate legal person.
How much does it cost to rent a small unit in Blackpool?

At The Rock Factory, ground-floor units run from £65 a week for 150 sq ft to £130 a week for the 300 sq ft two-storey unit. You pay one month's rent in advance and a deposit of one month's rent to move in.
Where can I get free business advice locally?

Blackpool Council's business pages are a good starting point for local licensing and rates. For tax, GOV.UK and HMRC's guidance cover most first questions, and an accountant can help with anything specific.

pages.title: Business Rates for Small Units | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: How business rates work for small units in Blackpool: rateable value, Small Business Rate Relief, who to ask and how to budget for 2026/27.
pages.lead: Business rates are the property tax on most commercial premises, and they worry a lot of people moving into their first unit. Here is how they work, why many small businesses pay little or nothing, and what to check before you sign.

sections.html:
Business rates are charged on most non-domestic property in England, such as shops, offices, workshops and units. They are collected by the local council, which in our case is Blackpool Council, and they are separate from your rent.

Your bill is based on the property's rateable value, not on your turnover or profit. Two businesses in identical units will normally be assessed the same way, whatever they earn.

Whether rates apply to a particular space depends on how it is assessed. That is why, for any unit you are considering, the right first question is simply: does this unit have its own rateable value, and who is liable for the bill?

It helps to separate three costs that people often blur together: rent, which goes to the landlord; utilities such as electricity; and business rates, which go to the council. Budget for each one on its own line.

sections.h2: Rateable value and who sets it
sections.html:
Rateable value is set by the Valuation Office Agency (VOA), not by the council or your landlord. It is the VOA's estimate of the yearly rent the property could have been let for on the open market at a fixed valuation date.

The council then works out your bill by multiplying the rateable value by a figure called the multiplier, and deducting any reliefs you are entitled to.

  1. Find the rateable valueYou can look up a property's rateable value on GOV.UK using the address.
  2. Check the multiplierThe council's business rates pages explain which multiplier applies for the current year.
  3. Apply any reliefSmall Business Rate Relief and other reliefs reduce the bill, sometimes to zero.

If you think a rateable value is wrong, GOV.UK explains how to check and challenge it with the VOA.

Small Business Rate Relief is the reason many sole traders and micro businesses in small units pay much less than they feared. It is aimed at businesses that occupy one property, or one main property plus small additional ones, with a low rateable value.

The 2026/27 position

For the 2026/27 tax year, GOV.UK and Blackpool Council describe 100% relief for eligible properties with a rateable value up to £12,000, with relief tapering for values a little above that. Thresholds and multipliers can change each April, so check the current figures on GOV.UK before you rely on them.

A few points catch people out:

  • You usually have to apply for relief. It is not always applied automatically.
  • Taking on a second property can affect your relief, so check the rules before you expand.
  • You must keep paying any bill you receive while the council considers your application.

Blackpool Council lets you apply for reliefs and report changes online through its business rates pages.

sections.h2: Business rates at The Rock Factory
sections.html:
Business rates may apply to our commercial units. Because liability depends on how each space is assessed, we would rather tell you about the specific unit than give a blanket answer that might not fit. Ask us about the unit you are interested in before you move in, and we will tell you what we know.

If you are budgeting now, list the costs you know for certain first. The 150 sq ft unit is £65 a week, or about £282 a month. The 160 sq ft unit is £69 a week, about £299 a month. The 180 sq ft unit is £78 a week, about £338 a month. Electricity is charged at the supplier rate with no markup, and there are no utility deposits. Our prices explained page breaks this down further.

Even if you expect relief, it is sensible to plan as though a bill could arrive. Here is a calm way to do it.

  1. Ask the landlord firstFind out whether the unit has its own rateable value and whether you will be liable.
  2. Look up the valueUse the GOV.UK service to see the current rateable value, if there is one.
  3. Check your eligibilityRead the Small Business Rate Relief rules for the current year and see whether you qualify.
  4. Apply promptlyContact Blackpool Council's business rates team as soon as you take on the property.
  5. Keep a bufferHold back a little each month until you have a confirmed position in writing.

If you currently work from home, GOV.UK says you would not normally pay business rates for using a small part of your home as an office, as long as you do not sell to visiting customers, employ people there or make non-domestic alterations. Moving to a unit changes that picture, which is one reason our guide to moving your business out of home asks you to check rates early.

Rates are about the property, not what you keep in it. If you mainly need storage rather than a workspace, ask how the space you are looking at is treated.

Whatever your situation, keep any letters from the council or the VOA together with your tenancy paperwork. If your circumstances change, for example you move to a larger unit, you will need them.

sections.h2: Questions to ask before you sign
sections.html:
Rates surprises usually come from questions nobody asked at the start. Put these to any landlord, in writing if you can, before you commit to a unit, shop or office.

  • Is this space assessed on its own, or as part of a larger property?
  • If it is assessed on its own, what is the current rateable value?
  • Will the bill come to me, or is it handled another way?
  • Has the previous occupier claimed any relief that I should know about?
  • If I rent two adjoining units, how would that be treated?

The last question matters because combining spaces, or taking on a second property, can change both the assessment and your eligibility for relief. Get a clear picture first, then speak to Blackpool Council's business rates team with the details. They deal with these questions every day and would rather help you get it right at the start than sort it out later.

This is general information, not legal or tax advice. Business rates rules, multipliers and relief thresholds are set by government and can change from year to year. Always check GOV.UK and Blackpool Council for the current position, and speak to the council's business rates team or a qualified adviser about your own property.

faqs: Do I pay business rates on a small unit?

It depends on whether the unit has its own rateable value and who is liable. Many small businesses on low rateable values qualify for Small Business Rate Relief. Ask the landlord about the specific unit, then check with Blackpool Council.
Is Small Business Rate Relief automatic?
Not always. You may need to apply to the council. Blackpool Council has an online route for applying for reliefs and reporting changes.
Who decides the rateable value?
The Valuation Office Agency sets rateable values. The council uses that figure to calculate the bill. If you think the value is wrong, GOV.UK explains how to challenge it.
Are business rates included in Rock Factory rent?
No. Rent covers the unit, and electricity usage is charged separately at the supplier rate. Business rates may apply to commercial units, so ask us about the unit you want.

pages.title: Moving Your Business Out of Home | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: When to move your business out of home, how to compare costs, and a step-by-step plan for moving into a small unit in Blackpool without the stress.
h1: out of home and into a unit
pages.lead: Working from home is cheap and convenient, until it is not. This guide helps you spot the moment to move, compare the real costs, and plan a move that does not interrupt your work.

sections.html:
Very few people decide to move out on a whim. It usually builds up over months. If several of these sound familiar, it is worth doing the sums.

  • Stock, packaging or tools have spread beyond one room.
  • You turn down bigger jobs or orders because there is nowhere to put them.
  • Family life and work keep getting in each other's way.
  • You avoid noisy or messy tasks because of neighbours.
  • You would like clients to visit, but not your house.
  • Couriers, deliveries and parcels have taken over the hallway.

There is also a quieter sign: you stop switching off. When work is always in the next room, it is hard to leave it. A separate place to go each morning can do as much for your head as for your business.

Money is a sign too. If you are paying for a garage, a friend's spare room or several small storage spaces just to keep the business going, bringing everything under one roof may cost less than you think.

Before comparing costs, make sure your current set-up is not quietly breaking a rule. GOV.UK points out that you may need permission from your mortgage lender or landlord to run a business from home, and planning permission if you make major changes.

Home insurance is another common gap. Many household policies do not cover business stock, tools or visitors, so check your policy wording. If you find a problem here, it can tip the decision towards moving out sooner.

Working from home is not free. You already pay for heat, light and space, and as a sole trader you may claim a share of those costs as business expenses. GOV.UK sets out a simplified flat rate based on hours worked at home, or you can work out the actual business proportion. Moving out replaces that with rent and running costs, which are usually allowable business expenses too.

Cost to compareWorking from homeSmall unit
RentNoneWeekly or monthly rent
ElectricityPart of the household billMetered usage, often separate
InsuranceMay need a business add-onYour own contents and liability cover
Business ratesNot normally for a small home officeMay apply, ask about the unit
TravelNoneDaily journey
Lost workJobs turned down for lack of spaceRoom to take them on

The last row matters most. If more space lets you take one extra job or a bigger order each month, it may cover the rent on its own.

sections.h2: What to look for in your first space
sections.html:
Your first premises should solve today's problem without locking you in. Look for flexibility above everything else.

  • Short, rolling terms with a clear notice period.
  • Electricity and internet already connected, so you can start straight away.
  • Access at the hours you actually work.
  • Wide access for bulky items, such as a roller shutter.
  • A landlord who will let you move to a bigger or smaller space later.
  • Clear rules about what activities are allowed.

At The Rock Factory, terms are rolling monthly with one month's notice after the first month, and you can swap to a bigger or smaller unit any time, subject to availability. Lighting, electricity and Wi-Fi are already connected, and there is 24-hour access. Our rental terms spell out the details.

sections.h2: A simple plan for the move
sections.html:
1. Measure what you haveList your stock, shelving, tools and furniture. It tells you what size you need, and what to leave behind.
  2. Pick the sizeUse the storage unit size guide and allow room to work, not just to store.
  3. Sort the paperworkArrange insurance from your move-in date, and update your address with suppliers, customers and HMRC where needed.
  4. Move in stagesShelving first, then stock, then the things you use every day. Keep trading throughout.
  5. Tell your customersUpdate your website, social profiles and Google Business Profile once you are settled.

Moving in costs at The Rock Factory are one month's rent in advance and a security deposit equal to one month's rent. You will also need valid government-issued photo ID and a signed Direct Debit mandate.

Give yourself a few weeks to settle before judging whether it worked. Track whether you take on more work, how much time you save, and how you feel at the end of each day.

Your new address can help customers find you. Tenants may use the Rock Factory address on their Google Business Profile, and our Google Business Profile address guide explains how to do it properly. If you also have visitors, read our guide to health and safety in a small unit.

Finally, review your insurance once you are in. Tell your home insurer that business stock has left the house, and make sure your new business cover starts on the day you move, not the day you remember.

sections.h2: What changes when you leave home
sections.html:
Moving out is not just a change of address. A few practical things shift at the same time, and it helps to expect them.

Your routine

You gain a commute, however short, and a clear start and end to the working day. Most people find this helps them focus, but plan when you will do admin, as it is easy to leave it for evenings at home.

Your records

If you used the flat rate or a proportion of household bills for working from home, that calculation changes when your main workplace moves. Your accountant or GOV.UK's expenses guidance will help you adjust.

Your visibility

A proper business address makes it easier to appear in local searches and to receive deliveries and clients without sharing your home address.

This is general information, not legal, tax or insurance advice. Rules on home working, expenses and business rates are set by government and lenders, and your own mortgage, tenancy or insurance terms may differ. Check the official guidance and your own documents, and ask an accountant or broker if you are unsure.

faqs: Can I claim my unit rent as a business expense?
Rent for premises used wholly for your business is generally an allowable expense for the self-employed. GOV.UK explains allowable expenses, and an accountant can confirm how it applies to you.
Will my home insurance cover business stock?
Often it does not, or only in a limited way. Read your policy wording or ask your insurer, especially if you keep stock or tools at home or have clients visit.
How do I know what size unit I need?
List what you will store and what work you will do there, then add space to move around. Many people moving out of a spare room start with around 150 to 180 sq ft and swap later if needed.
Can I still work from home some days?
Of course. Plenty of tenants use a unit for stock, tools and client visits while doing admin at home. With 24-hour access, you can go in whenever it suits you.
What do I need to move into a Rock Factory unit?
One month's rent in advance, a security deposit equal to one month's rent, valid government-issued photo ID and a signed Direct Debit mandate. Pre-bookings get the first week free.

pages.title: Google Business Profile Address Guide | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: How to list a unit address on your Google Business Profile in Blackpool: storefront vs service area, Google's rules, verification and common mistakes.
h1: and how to get it right
pages.lead: For most local businesses, Google Maps is the shop window. The address you give Google decides where you appear and whether your profile survives. Here is how to list a unit address properly, in line with Google's own guidelines.

sections.h2: Why the address matters so much
sections.html:
When someone near Park Road searches for a repairer, a framer or a dog groomer, Google leans heavily on location to decide which businesses to show. A real, verified address in Blackpool helps you appear in those searches. A vague or borrowed address can hold you back, or get your profile suspended.

Many people working from home avoid listing an address because they do not want strangers at the door. Moving into a unit changes that. You can show a proper business address without giving away where you live.

Your address also appears in other places that feed into local search, such as directories, your website footer and social media pages. Getting it right on Google first gives you a reference version to copy everywhere else.

Google treats businesses in two broad ways, and you need to pick the one that matches how you really work.

Storefront, where customers come to you

If customers visit you at the address, for collections, fittings, repairs or appointments, you can show the address publicly. Google's guidelines expect the location to be staffed during the hours you list and able to receive customers.

Service area, where you go to customers

If you travel to customers, such as a gardener, cleaner or mobile mechanic, Google expects you to hide your address and show the areas you serve instead. The address still matters for verification and ranking, it just is not displayed.

Some businesses are a mix of both. Google allows a hybrid set-up where you show the address and also list service areas, provided you do receive customers there.

Google publishes guidelines for representing your business, and they are worth reading in full. The points that matter most for a small unit are these:

  • Use the precise, real address where your business operates, including the unit number.
  • Your business should be able to make in-person contact with customers during its stated hours.
  • Use your real-world business name, without extra keywords or locations added.
  • Keep hours, phone number and categories accurate and up to date.
  • Virtual offices, where you rent a mailing address but do not operate there, are not eligible.
  • PO boxes and mailboxes at remote locations are not acceptable addresses.
  • A coworking address is only eligible in limited circumstances, such as clear signage and your own staff present during business hours.

The common thread is simple: Google wants the pin on the map to be somewhere customers could genuinely find you.

Tenants may use the Rock Factory address on their Google Business Profile. Because you rent a real unit and work from it, you are not in the virtual office situation that Google excludes. You can also receive mail and clients at the unit, and there is 24-hour access, so you can set opening hours that match when you are actually there.

Format your address clearly and consistently, for example with your unit number, then The Old Rock Factory, Keswick Road, Blackpool FY1 5PB. Use exactly the same wording on your website, invoices and social profiles. Consistency helps Google trust that the details are correct.

If you want to put up a sign to help customers and support verification, ask us first about what is possible.

Think about your opening hours honestly. If you are at your unit by appointment only, say so in your profile description rather than listing hours when nobody will be there.

Google asks most new or moved profiles to verify that the business is real and at the address given. The method varies, and Google decides which options to offer you.

  1. Set up the profileEnter your business name, category and address exactly as they appear in real life.
  2. Choose a verification methodFollow the options Google offers. Some involve recording a short video of your premises and business.
  3. Show you trade thereIf filming, show the location, your equipment or stock, and anything that proves you run the business, such as branded materials.
  4. Wait, then checkReviews can take a few days. Do not keep editing the address while you wait, as that can restart checks.

Because our units are windowless and enclosed, good lighting in your video helps. Open the roller shutter or door so the entrance and surroundings are visible as well as the inside.

• Adding "Blackpool" or a service keyword to your business name when it is not part of your real name.
  • Showing an address for a service-area business that never receives customers.
  • Listing hours when nobody is there to answer the door.
  • Creating a second profile for the same business at a new address instead of updating the first.
  • Using different address formats on different websites.

If you are moving an existing profile from home to a unit, edit the address on your current profile rather than starting again, so you keep your reviews. Our tenant IceWork can help with this kind of thing, and their web design page explains their tenant offer.

A profile is not a one-off job. Google rewards businesses that keep their information accurate and active, and customers notice when a listing looks neglected.

  1. Add real photosShow your work, your products and the entrance, so visitors know what to look for when they arrive at Keswick Road.
  2. Answer reviewsThank people for good ones and reply calmly to criticism. Future customers read the replies.
  3. Update hoursChange your hours for holidays and quiet periods, so nobody arrives at a closed door.
  4. Post occasionallyShare new products, offers or finished jobs. It keeps the profile looking current.

If clients will visit you, our find us page is a useful link to send them alongside your own directions.

This is general information, not legal advice or official guidance from Google. Google changes its policies and verification process from time to time, so read the current Business Profile guidelines before you set up or change a listing. Google, not us, decides whether a profile is approved.

faqs: Can I use a storage unit address on Google Maps?

Only if you genuinely operate your business there in a way that fits Google's guidelines. A unit you work from and receive customers at is very different from a virtual office address, which Google does not allow.
Can Rock Factory tenants use the building address?
Yes. Tenants may use the Rock Factory address on their Google Business Profile. Include your unit number and keep the format the same everywhere.
Should I hide my address if I work at customers' homes?
Google expects service-area businesses that do not serve customers at their address to hide it and list service areas instead. If customers also visit you, a hybrid profile may suit.
Will I lose my reviews if I move address?
Not if you update the address on your existing profile. Creating a new profile instead can split or lose your reviews.
How long does verification take?
It varies. Google sets the method and timings, and some checks take a few days. Avoid changing details while a review is in progress.

Business eligibility and ownership guidelines (Google Business Profile Help)

pages.title: Small Business Insurance Guide | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: A plain-English guide to insurance for small businesses in Blackpool: public liability, employers' liability, stock, tools and what a unit tenant needs.
pages.lead: Insurance is one of those jobs that is easy to put off and painful to get wrong. This guide explains the main types of cover small businesses consider, the one that is compulsory once you employ people, and what to think about when you rent a unit.

sections.h2: Start with your risks, not a product list
sections.html:
Insurers sell dozens of products, and it is easy to buy cover you do not need while missing the one you do. A better starting point is to write down what could realistically go wrong in your business.

  • Could a customer or member of the public be hurt, or their property damaged, because of your work?
  • Could something you make or sell cause harm after it leaves you?
  • What would it cost to replace your tools, equipment or stock tomorrow?
  • Could advice or design work you give lead to a client losing money?
  • How long could you survive if you could not trade for a month?

Take that list to a broker or insurer. It leads to a far better conversation than asking for "business insurance".

It also helps to know your numbers. Add up the replacement cost of everything in your unit, then estimate how much income you would lose in a month off. Those two figures guide the cover limits you need far better than guesswork.

sections.h2: Employers' liability: the one that is compulsory
sections.html:
If you employ people, GOV.UK says you must have employers' liability insurance from an authorised insurer as soon as you become an employer. It covers claims from employees who are injured or become ill because of their work.

Check the GOV.UK rules

GOV.UK currently states that the policy must cover you for at least £5 million and that you can be fined for every day you are not properly insured. There are limited exemptions, for example some businesses that only employ close family members, but these do not apply to limited companies. Read the official page before assuming an exemption fits you.

If you are a sole trader with no employees, this does not usually apply. It is worth revisiting the moment you take on even part-time help.

sections.h2: Other covers small businesses commonly consider
sections.html:
Public liability

Covers claims from members of the public who are injured or whose property is damaged because of your business. It is not a legal requirement in general, but many customers, venues and markets ask to see it.

Product liability

Relevant if you make, modify or sell physical products. It covers claims that something you supplied caused injury or damage.

Contents, tools and stock

Covers your own equipment and goods against theft, fire and damage, at your premises and sometimes in transit or at events.

Professional indemnity

For businesses that give advice or design work. It covers claims that your work caused a client financial loss.

Business interruption

Helps replace lost income if an insured event stops you trading for a while.

Vans used for work also need the right class of motor insurance. Check that your policy covers business use, and carrying goods or tools if you do.

sections.h2: Insurance when you rent a unit
sections.html:
When you rent premises, the landlord normally insures the building. That cover is for the structure, not for your belongings or your business. Your own stock, tools and equipment need your own cover, and so does your liability to visitors you invite in.

At The Rock Factory, insurance for your contents is not included in the rent, so arrange your own before you move in. The building's insurance is also the reason some uses are not allowed, including car storage and activities such as melting waxes or plastics, so check that your planned use has been approved.

For storage-only tenants, our separate storage insurance guide looks at insuring goods in store.

sections.h2: Tell your insurer the full picture
sections.html:
Many claims are reduced or refused because the insurer was not told something important. When you take out or renew cover, be clear about these points:

  1. Where you workGive the full premises address and say whether it is a unit, a shop or your home.
  2. What you do thereDescribe your activities accurately, including any tools or machinery.
  3. When you are thereMention if you work alone or late at night.
  4. What you keep thereGive a realistic replacement value for stock and equipment.
  5. What security there isDescribe it accurately. At The Rock Factory, that means a free CCTV app covering the entrance and the area outside the units.

Update your insurer when anything changes, including moving out of home or taking on staff.

Cheapest is not always best value. Compare the excess, the limits for single items, whether cover applies away from your premises, and any conditions about locks or alarms. A broker who knows small businesses can be worth it if your activities are unusual.

Keep a simple folder with your policies, renewal dates and an up-to-date list of equipment with photos and receipts. It makes claims faster and renewals easier.

Diarise your renewal date a month in advance. That gives you time to review what has changed in your business, get comparison quotes and avoid an automatic renewal at a higher price. If you have made a claim, keep the correspondence with your policy documents for future reference.

Every business is different, but some patterns are common. Use these as prompts for your conversation with an insurer, not as a checklist to buy from.

BusinessCovers often discussed
Online sellerStock, goods in transit, product liability
Maker or crafterTools, materials, product liability, cover at fairs
RepairerCustomers' goods in your care, tools, public liability
TradespersonPublic liability, tools in the van, employers' liability if you have staff
Consultant or designerProfessional indemnity, office contents, cyber

One cover people often forget is goods belonging to customers. If you repair phones, reupholster chairs or service bikes, you may be holding valuable items that are not yours. Check that your policy covers them while they are in your unit.

This is general information, not insurance or legal advice. We are not an insurer or broker and cannot recommend specific products. Policy terms vary widely, so read the documents carefully and speak to an authorised insurer or broker about your own business. Check GOV.UK for the current employers' liability rules.

faqs: Is public liability insurance a legal requirement?

Not in general. It is often requested by customers, venues and market organisers, and many small businesses choose it for peace of mind. Employers' liability is the one GOV.UK lists as compulsory once you employ people.
Does The Rock Factory insure my stock?
No. Insurance for your contents is not included in the rent, so arrange your own cover for stock, tools and equipment before you move in.
Do I need employers' liability if I only use freelancers?
It depends on the working relationship. GOV.UK explains who counts as an employee for this purpose, so check the guidance or ask an insurer.
Why is car storage not allowed in Rock Factory units?
Because of the building's insurance. It is one of a few uses we cannot permit, alongside activities like melting waxes or plastics and bulk flammable liquids.
Will my insurer want to know about the CCTV?

Insurers usually ask about security. Describe it accurately: at The Rock Factory, that is a free app giving access to CCTV covering the entrance and the area outside the units, plus your own lockable roller shutter or security door. Do not claim alarms or other features that are not there.

pages.title: Health and Safety in a Small Unit | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: Health and safety for small business units in Blackpool: risk assessments, fire safety, electrics, working alone and first aid, scaled to a small team.
pages.lead: Health and safety law applies to small businesses too, but it is meant to be proportionate. For a one or two person unit, it mostly means thinking ahead, keeping things tidy and knowing what to do if something goes wrong.

sections.html:
The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) has a section of its website called "health and safety made simple" for exactly this kind of business. Its message is reassuring: you need to manage the real risks of your work, not fill folders with forms.

That still applies if you are self-employed. Your duties cover you, anyone you employ, and anyone else affected by your work, such as customers, neighbouring tenants and delivery drivers.

A good way to start is to ask yourself one question at the end of each day: if someone else walked into my unit right now, could they get hurt? If the honest answer is yes, fix that first. Most improvements in a small unit cost very little, such as a hook for a cable, a shelf for a heavy box or a lid on a bin.

A risk assessment is just a structured look at what could cause harm in your work and what you do about it.

  1. Spot the hazardsWalk round your unit. Think about tools, trailing cables, heavy lifting, dust, chemicals and trip hazards.
  2. Decide who could be harmedYou, any staff, visitors and other tenants passing your door.
  3. Control the risksRemove the hazard if you can. If not, guard it, store it better or change how you work.
  4. Record what mattersHSE says that if you have fewer than five workers you do not have to write it down, though it is useful to do so.
  5. Review itLook again when you add new equipment, take on staff or change what you do.

Fire safety in workplaces is covered by its own law. GOV.UK explains that the "responsible person" for premises must carry out and regularly review a fire risk assessment, keep a written record of it, and plan for an emergency. In a shared building, more than one person can have responsibilities, and they need to work together.

In practice, for your own unit:

  • Keep your exit route clear at all times, inside and outside the unit.
  • Do not stack stock against doors or across walkways.
  • Keep combustible waste such as cardboard and offcuts under control.
  • Know where the nearest way out of the building is.

Some activities carry too much fire risk for our building. At The Rock Factory, we do not allow melting or heating combustibles such as waxes, plastics, resins or oils, bulk flammable liquids or gases unless agreed in writing, or cooking and hot food. Low-risk materials like wood, paper, card, fabric and dry goods are fine.

Every Rock Factory unit has lighting and standard single-phase electricity already connected. There is no three-phase supply, so check your equipment's requirements before you buy.

The law requires electrical equipment that could cause injury to be kept in a safe condition. HSE is clear that this does not automatically mean a yearly portable appliance test. In a low-risk setting, regular user checks and visual inspections often do most of the work, with testing where the risk justifies it.

  • Check plugs, leads and casings for damage before use.
  • Avoid daisy-chaining extension leads or overloading sockets.
  • Switch off and unplug heat-producing tools when you leave.
  • Take damaged kit out of use straight away.

With 24-hour access, many tenants work early mornings, evenings or weekends when nobody else is about. HSE's lone working guidance says employers must manage the risks before people work alone, and the same thinking is sensible if you are self-employed.

  • Tell someone when you arrive and when you expect to leave.
  • Keep your phone charged and with you, not in the van.
  • Save the riskiest tasks, such as using power tools or heavy lifting, for times when someone else is around.
  • Use the free CCTV app to check the entrance and outside area before arriving or leaving.

If you employ someone who will work alone, include that in your risk assessment and agree a simple check-in routine, such as a message at set times.

HSE expects every workplace to have suitable first aid arrangements. For a small, low-risk unit, that usually means a stocked first aid kit and knowing who will take charge if something happens. Keep the kit where you can reach it quickly.

Shared facilities at The Rock Factory include toilets, water and a tea and coffee room, so you have somewhere to take a proper break away from your bench.

Manual handling causes many workplace injuries. Use trolleys, split heavy loads and get help with awkward items. A roller-shutter unit makes it easier to bring large things in at ground level.

Many small businesses use products that need a little care: cleaning chemicals, glues, water-based finishes, aerosol sprays and the dust from sanding or cutting. The law on hazardous substances, known as COSHH, expects you to understand what you use and control exposure.

  • Read the safety data sheet or label before you use a new product.
  • Choose the least hazardous product that does the job.
  • Keep only the quantity you need in the unit, with lids firmly on.
  • Use gloves, eye protection or a mask where the label says to.
  • Store products away from heat and out of reach of visitors.

Bulk flammable liquids, such as fuel or solvent-based paints and chemicals, and gas cylinders are not allowed in our building unless agreed in writing. If your work needs them, raise it before you move in.

Visitors and clients

If customers come to your unit, think about them too. Keep the area by your door clear, put sharp tools away before they arrive, and do not let them wander into a working area while machines are running.

This is general information, not legal or professional health and safety advice. Your duties depend on your activities, your staff and your premises. Use the HSE and GOV.UK guidance linked below, and get competent help if your work involves significant hazards such as machinery or hazardous substances.

faqs: Do I need a written risk assessment as a sole trader?
HSE says you do not have to write it down if you have fewer than five workers, but it is still useful. You do still need to think through the risks and control them.
Do I need my tools PAT tested every year?

HSE says the law does not require annual PAT testing. It requires equipment to be maintained safely, which for low-risk kit is often done through user checks and visual inspections, with testing where needed.
Who does the fire risk assessment in a shared building?

There can be more than one responsible person. The building owner handles shared areas, and you should think about fire risks in your own unit and how they fit the building's arrangements. Ask us if you are unsure.
Can I use a heater in my unit?
Ask us first. Heat-producing equipment needs care in any enclosed space, and some uses involving heat are not permitted in the building.
What should be in a first aid kit for a small unit?

HSE says the contents should reflect your own assessment of needs. For a low-risk unit, a standard workplace kit is a sensible start, with extras such as eye wash if you work with dust or liquids. Check it every few months and replace anything used or out of date.
sources: Managing risks and risk assessment at work (HSE)
Fire safety in the workplace: who's responsible (GOV.UK)
Fire safety in the workplace: fire risk assessments (GOV.UK)
Lone working: protect those working alone (HSE)

pages.title: Business Unit vs Shop vs Coworking | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: Should your Blackpool business rent a small unit, a shop or a coworking desk? An honest comparison of cost, flexibility, storage and customers.
pages.lead: When a business outgrows home, the three usual options are a small unit, a shop or a coworking desk. Each is right for some businesses and wrong for others. This guide helps you work out which one fits the way you actually work.

sections.html:
The best premises are the ones that match your daily routine. Before looking at prices, answer four questions honestly.

  • Do customers need to find you by walking past, or do they come by arrangement?
  • Do you need space for stock, tools or materials, or just a laptop?
  • Do you make noise, mess or dust?
  • When do you work: office hours, or early, late and at weekends?

Your answers usually point clearly at one option.

Be honest about the future too. If you expect to hire someone within a year, take on more stock or start running workshops, choose a space that can grow with you, or terms flexible enough to let you move without penalty.

sections.h2: The three options side by side
sections.html:
FactorSmall unitHigh street shopCoworking
Passing tradeLittle or noneYes, the main benefitNone
Storage for stock and toolsYesSome, often limitedUsually very little
Messy or noisy workOften possible, with approvalDepends on the leaseRarely
Typical commitmentOften flexibleOften a longer leaseOften flexible
Fit-out costLowCan be highNone
Company and networkingSome, from other tenantsCustomersPlenty

These are general patterns. Individual properties vary, so always read the actual terms.

A shop earns its higher costs when people buying on impulse are a big part of your sales. Gift shops, cafes and some services live on footfall. In a seaside town, that footfall can also be strongly seasonal, which our guide to running a seasonal business in Blackpool looks at in more detail.

The trade-offs are usually commitment and overheads. Shop leases are often longer, and you may be responsible for repairs, shopfitting and business rates. Before you sign, GOV.UK's guidance on renting business property explains the main tenant responsibilities, and a solicitor should review any lease.

Coworking suits people whose business fits in a laptop bag: designers, consultants, bookkeepers and remote workers. You get a desk, internet, company and often meeting rooms, without managing a property.

It works less well if you hold stock, use tools or need privacy for client work. Shared spaces also have house rules about noise, phone calls and hours. If you want to appear on Google Maps from a coworking address, note that Google only accepts that in limited circumstances.

sections.h2: When a small unit makes sense
sections.html:
A unit is the practical middle ground. You get a private, lockable space for stock and tools, room to do hands-on work, and the freedom to come and go when you like, without paying for a shop front you do not need.

Units suit online sellers, repairers, makers, tradespeople and anyone whose customers come by appointment or never visit at all. The trade-off is visibility: you will need to bring customers to you through your website, Google and word of mouth.

At The Rock Factory, ground-floor units run from 150 sq ft at £65 a week to a 300 sq ft two-storey unit with an upstairs room at £130 a week. All have lighting, electricity and Wi-Fi connected, 24-hour access and rolling monthly terms. Two separate offices at £70 a week each are being refurbished for January 2027, if a desk-based space suits you better.

Comparing weekly rents alone can mislead. Build a full monthly picture for each option.

  1. RentConvert everything to the same period. A weekly figure times 52, divided by 12, gives the monthly equivalent.
  2. UtilitiesCheck whether electricity, internet and water are included, metered or extra.
  3. Rates and service chargesAsk whether business rates apply and whether any service charge is added.
  4. Set-upDeposits, fit-out, signage and moving costs.
  5. ExitHow much notice you must give, and any costs to leave.

Our prices explained page shows how this works for our units, and our guide to business rates for small units covers the rates question.

You do not have to pick only one. Some businesses keep a unit for stock and production and sell through markets or pop-ups. Others work from home most days and use a unit for tools, deliveries and client visits. Starting with flexible space means you can change course without being tied to a long lease.

Whatever you choose, revisit the decision every six months or so. A business that needed a desk last year might need a workshop now, and the reverse happens too. The right premises are the ones that suit you today, with an easy way out when they no longer do.

Real decisions are rarely neat, so here are three typical situations and how the choice often plays out.

The online seller

Sales happen on a marketplace, and nobody needs to visit. The priority is somewhere to store, pack and photograph stock. A shop would be paying for footfall that never comes, and coworking has no room for boxes. A small unit with a roller shutter for courier collections fits naturally.

The bookkeeper

The work is a laptop and the occasional client meeting. There is no stock and no mess. Coworking or a small office makes sense here, with a meeting room booked when needed.

The furniture restorer

Needs a bench, tools and space for pieces in progress, but also wants customers to see finished work. A unit for the workshop, with selling through markets, social media and occasional pop-ups, often beats paying shop rent year round.

If you see yourself in one of these, the small business unit ideas page has more examples of what works from a unit.

This is general information, not legal or financial advice. Leases and licences vary widely, and the comparisons above are typical patterns rather than rules. Read any agreement carefully and get professional advice before signing a commercial lease.

faqs: Is a small unit cheaper than a shop?
Often, because you are not paying for a prime frontage, though it depends on the properties you compare. Add up rent, utilities, rates and set-up costs for each before deciding.
Can customers visit me at a unit?
At The Rock Factory, yes. Tenants can receive clients and mail at the unit, which suits appointment-based businesses.
Can I run a retail shop from a Rock Factory unit?
All business use needs our prior approval. Units are windowless and set back from the street, so they suit appointment-based or online businesses better than walk-in retail. Ask us about your plans.
What if I outgrow my first space?

With flexible terms, you can move. At The Rock Factory, you can swap to a bigger or smaller unit any time, subject to availability, and some units have interconnecting doors so you can rent adjoining space.
Is coworking cheaper than a unit?

Not always. A desk can look cheap per day, but costs add up if you are there full time, and you may still need to pay for storage elsewhere. Compare the full monthly cost for the way you would actually use each space.
Can I use a unit as an office?
Yes, if it suits you, though our ground-floor units are windowless. If you want a dedicated office, two separate offices at £70 a week each are being refurbished for January 2027.
sources: Guidelines for representing your business on Google (Google Business Profile Help)

pages.title: How to Set Up a Small Workshop | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: Practical tips for setting up a small workshop unit in Blackpool: layout, single-phase power, storage walls, dust control and what materials are allowed.
h1: How to set up a small workshop
pages.lead: A small workshop lives or dies by its layout. With a bit of planning, 150 to 300 sq ft is enough for a surprising amount of making, mending and building. Here is how to set one up so it is safe, tidy and pleasant to work in.

sections.html:
Before you carry anything in, sketch the floor plan. Note where the door or roller shutter is, where the sockets are, and where the light falls. Then list every tool and piece of furniture you plan to bring, with rough sizes.

Think about the way work flows through the space. Materials come in, get cut or prepared, get assembled or repaired, then get finished and stored or sent out. Arrange your stations in that order, so you are not walking back and forth across the room all day.

Leave clear floor space in front of each tool for safe operation, and keep a clear route from the back of the unit to the exit.

Mark out heights as well as floor space. Tall racking along the back wall, a bench at a comfortable working height and a clear space under it for offcuts bins all help a small room work harder. Measure the roller shutter or door opening too, so you know the largest piece you can bring in or take out.

The type of access matters as much as the size. A roller shutter lets you bring in sheet materials, large furniture or a heavy machine without wrestling them through a doorway. A personnel door is better if your work is small-scale and you value a more office-like feel.

UnitAccessWeekly rentGood for
150 sq ftRoller shutter£65A single bench and tool wall
160 sq ftSecurity door£69Repairs, electronics, small crafts
180 sq ftRoller shutter£78Bench plus a larger machine
300 sq ft two-storeyRoller shutter£130Workshop below, office or storage above

Some units have interconnecting doors, so you can rent two or three side by side. Side-by-side units can give you both roller-shutter and personnel-door access.

Every Rock Factory unit has lighting and standard single-phase electricity connected. There is no three-phase supply, so if you are buying a large saw, compressor or lathe, check that a single-phase version exists and suits your work.

  • Plan your bench positions around the sockets to keep cables off the floor.
  • Use one good-quality extension per area rather than chains of cheap ones.
  • Avoid running several high-draw tools at once on the same circuit.
  • Fit a switch-off routine into the end of each day.

Electricity usage is charged separately at the supplier rate with no markup, so energy-efficient tools and LED task lights pay you back over time.

sections.h2: Use the walls, keep the floor clear
sections.html:
In a small workshop, floor space is precious and wall space is often wasted. Get things up and off the floor.

  • Freestanding shelving for boxed stock and materials.
  • Pegboard or slatted panels above the bench for hand tools.
  • Labelled clear boxes for fixings and small parts.
  • Mobile bases for heavy tools, so you can roll them out of the way.
  • A fold-down or wall-mounted bench if you need flexible floor space.

Ask us before fixing anything to the walls, as we will want to agree how it is done.

Dust is the hidden hazard in many workshops, especially woodworking. HSE treats wood dust as a hazardous substance that can cause long-term health effects, including occupational asthma, and recommends capturing it at source.

  1. Capture it at the toolUse on-tool extraction or a suitable dust extractor connected to sanders and saws.
  2. Clean with a vacuumHSE advises against dry sweeping or using compressed air to clean up dust.
  3. Protect your lungsFor the dustiest jobs, a suitable mask or respirator adds protection.
  4. Air the spaceOur units are windowless, so open the shutter or door when you can while working.

Our guide to working in a windowless unit has more on lighting and air.

sections.h2: What you can and cannot do
sections.html:
All business use needs our prior approval, and some activities are not allowed in the building because of fire risk and insurance.

  • Wood, paper, card, fabric and dry goods are fine.
  • Repair work, assembly, upholstery, framing and similar crafts usually fit well.
  • Melting or heating combustibles such as waxes, plastics, resins or oils, which rules out candle and soap making, resin casting and 3D print farms.
  • Bulk flammable liquids or gases, such as fuel, solvent-based paints or gas cylinders, unless agreed in writing.
  • Cooking or hot food.
  • Car storage.

If you are not sure where your craft fits, message us on WhatsApp and describe what you plan to do before you commit.

You will share the building with other small businesses. Keep shared areas clear of offcuts and deliveries, take your waste away regularly, and give others a heads-up before a particularly noisy job. A little courtesy makes a shared building a much nicer place to work.

Keep your entrance area tidy, too. A clear doorway is safer, looks more professional to visiting customers, and makes it easy for couriers to collect and deliver.

sections.h2: Your first week in the workshop
sections.html:
It is tempting to move everything in on day one. A staged approach gets you working sooner and avoids having to shift heavy kit twice.

  1. Day one: the shellClean the floor, check where the sockets and lights are, and mark out your zones with tape.
  2. Day two: storagePut up shelving and racking before anything else, so tools have a home when they arrive.
  3. Day three: the benchInstall your main workbench and the tools you use most, then try a small job.
  4. Day four: adjustMove anything that felt awkward. You will learn more from one real job than from any plan.
  5. Day five: safetyAdd the first aid kit, a fire exit check and your end-of-day switch-off routine.

Keep a notebook of what you wish you had, and buy it once you have used the space for a few weeks. Workshops evolve, and the best ones are tuned to how their owner actually works.

This is general information, not professional health and safety advice. Machinery and dust control can carry real risks. Follow your tool manufacturers' instructions and HSE's woodworking and dust guidance, and get competent help to set up extraction or anything you are unsure about.

faqs: Can I run woodworking machinery in a unit?
Woodwork is a low-risk material use we can usually approve, but all business use needs prior approval. Supply is single-phase only, so check your machines before you buy.
Is there three-phase power?
No. Units have standard single-phase electricity only. Many workshop tools are available in single-phase versions.
Can I make candles or resin pieces in my workshop?
No. Melting or heating combustibles such as waxes, plastics, resins and oils is not allowed in the building.
How do I get large sheets or machines in?
Choose a roller-shutter unit. The 150 sq ft, 180 sq ft and two-storey units all have roller-shutter access.
Can I fix shelving to the walls?
Ask us first. Freestanding shelving is the easiest option, and if you want to fix anything to walls we will agree how it is done before you start.
sources: Managing risks and risk assessment at work (HSE)

pages.title: Working in a Windowless Unit | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: How to make a windowless business unit in Blackpool bright, comfortable and healthy to work in: lighting, fresh air, breaks, colour and routines.
pages.lead: Plenty of workshops, studios and stockrooms have no windows, and many people prefer the privacy and wall space. The trick is to plan the light, air and rhythm of your day so an enclosed space stays comfortable.

sections.html:
A windowless unit is not a compromise for everyone. It gives you four full walls for shelving and tool boards, steady light that does not glare on screens, privacy from passers-by and less to worry about when you leave stock behind.

Photographers, sellers who shoot product images and people who work with screens often prefer controlled light. Makers enjoy being able to fill every wall. The aim is to keep those benefits while avoiding the downsides.

A windowless room is also easier to keep at a steady temperature and free from sun damage. Fabrics, prints, paper and photographs stay out of direct sunlight, which helps them keep their colour.

Lighting is already connected in every Rock Factory unit. Think of it as a starting point and add to it for the work you do. HSE's guidance on lighting at work explains that lighting should be suitable for the task and should not create risks of its own.

  • Add task lights at each bench or desk, angled to avoid shadows from your own hands.
  • Choose a cooler, daylight-style colour for detailed work and colour matching.
  • Use warmer lamps in any break or seating corner.
  • Keep fittings clean and replace failing bulbs promptly.
  • Keep a torch by the door in case of a power cut.

LED lighting uses little electricity, which helps because usage is charged at the supplier rate.

Plan your light switches and lamps around how you move. Being able to light the doorway first, then your bench, makes arriving early or leaving late much more comfortable.

Air feels stale faster in a closed room. Build airflow into your routine rather than waiting until you notice it.

  1. Open up when you workLift the roller shutter or open the door for a few minutes regularly, more often during dusty or busy tasks.
  2. Move the airA simple fan helps circulate air when the door is open.
  3. Control the sourceCapture dust at the tool and avoid products with strong fumes.
  4. Dress for the seasonLayers are easier than fighting the temperature. Ask us before bringing in any heater.

Some activities are not suited to an enclosed room at all. In our building, that includes anything involving melting or heating combustibles, solvent-based products in bulk, and cooking.

The thing you miss most without a window is a sense of time passing. It is easy to look up and find it is dark outside. Build daylight into your day on purpose.

  • Take short breaks outside, even for five minutes.
  • Have lunch away from your bench, in daylight if possible.
  • Use a clock or timer so the hours do not slip by.
  • Make the most of the shared tea and coffee room for a change of scene.

If you work long hours with screens, regular screen breaks help your eyes as well as your mood.

Shared spaces help with the sense of isolation too. Chatting to other tenants over a cup of tea can be a welcome change from working on your own.

sections.h2: Make it a place you want to be
sections.html:
A blank room can feel bleak. Small touches go a long way. Light-coloured surfaces bounce light around. A rug or mat by the desk adds warmth. Pictures, a radio and a few low-light plants make it feel lived in. Keep work zones tidy so the space feels calm when you walk in.

Ask us before painting or fixing anything to walls, so we can agree how it is done.

Think about sound as well. A windowless room can feel very quiet, which is great for concentration but can feel isolating over a long day. Background music or a podcast helps some people, while others enjoy the calm. Find what keeps you working well.

sections.h2: If you really need a window
sections.html:
All our ground-floor units are windowless. If natural light matters for part of your work, the 300 sq ft two-storey unit has an upstairs office or storage area with a window, reached by an internal staircase, above a roller-shutter workshop space. It is £130 a week.

Many tenants find the windowless units suit them better than expected, especially for storage, online selling and making. You can compare every unit side by side to see which fits.

sections.h2: How different businesses make it work
sections.html:
The right set-up depends on what you do in the space.

Storage and stock rooms

If you mostly store and pack, windows are not much use and a windowless room is ideal. Bright overhead lighting, clear labelling and a small packing table near the door are usually all you need.

Makers and repairers

Detailed work needs strong, even light at the bench. A magnifier lamp helps for fine jobs. Airflow matters more if you sand, cut or glue, so plan dust control and open up regularly.

Desk-based work

For long hours at a screen, balance the screen brightness with the room so your eyes are not working against glare or gloom. A comfortable chair and a regular break routine matter more than you might expect.

Studios and photography

Controlled light is a gift here. Without daylight changing through the day, you can set lights once and get consistent results.

No windows means nobody can see what you keep inside, which many tenants value for stock and tools. With a roller shutter or security door and a free CCTV app covering the entrance and the area outside the units, you can check in from your phone when you are away.

For more on keeping a unit secure, read our storage security tips.

This is general information, not health or legal advice. If you employ people, you have duties about lighting, ventilation and temperature in the workplace, set out in HSE's guidance. Use the official guidance below and get competent advice if your work produces dust, fumes or heat.

faqs: Are all Rock Factory units windowless?
All the ground-floor units are windowless. The two-storey unit has an upstairs office or storage area with a window.
Is there lighting in the units?
Yes. Lighting, electricity and Wi-Fi are already connected in every unit. Many tenants add task lights for detailed work.
Can I work in a windowless unit all day?
Many people do, especially with good lighting, regular fresh air and breaks outside. Plan your day so you get daylight at least a few times.
Is a windowless unit good for product photography?
It can be. Controlled light without changing daylight makes it easier to get consistent photos, with your own lighting set-up.
Can I keep the roller shutter open while I work?
Opening up while you work is a simple way to bring in fresh air and light. Just keep your entrance tidy and clear for others.
Will I get enough light to do detailed work?

Lighting is connected in every unit, and most people add task lights at their bench or desk. A daylight-style lamp angled to avoid shadows makes fine work much easier. HSE's lighting guidance is a useful reference if you employ people.

pages.title: Sole Trader or Limited Company? | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: Sole trader or limited company? A plain-English comparison of paperwork, liability, tax and privacy for small businesses starting out in Blackpool.
pages.lead: It is one of the first questions every new business asks, and the honest answer is that it depends. This guide explains how each structure works day to day so you can have a more useful conversation with an accountant.

sections.html:
As a sole trader, you are the business. There is no legal separation between you and what you do. You keep the profits after tax, and you are personally responsible for any debts.

A limited company is a separate legal person. It is registered with Companies House, it owns its own money, and it has directors who run it and shareholders who own it. In a small business, that is often the same one person.

Partnerships and other structures exist too. GOV.UK has a short guide to choosing a legal structure that covers them all.

The choice is not permanent. You can change structure later, and many businesses do. What matters now is picking the one that fits your current size, risk and appetite for paperwork.

PointSole traderLimited company
Setting upRegister with HMRC for Self AssessmentRegister with Companies House, with identity checks for directors
LiabilityPersonally responsible for business debtsUsually limited to what you put in, with exceptions
TaxIncome tax and National Insurance on profitsCorporation Tax on company profits, then tax on what you take out
PaperworkRecords and a yearly tax returnCompany accounts, confirmation statement and company tax return
Public informationLittle is publishedSome details appear on the public register
Changing laterCan incorporate laterClosing a company takes formal steps

Most small businesses in Blackpool start this way because it is quick and cheap. You can trade under your own name or a business name, as long as it follows the naming rules on GOV.UK.

GOV.UK explains that you need to register for Self Assessment if your trading income goes over the trading allowance, and the deadline to register is 5 October after the end of the tax year you started. The trading allowance has been £1,000 a year for some time, but check GOV.UK for the tax year you are in.

  • Simple records and one tax return a year.
  • Profits are yours to use without formal paperwork.
  • Easy to stop if the business does not work out.

The main downside is personal liability. If the business owes money, creditors can pursue you personally. Insurance helps with some risks, but not all.

A limited company can make sense when profits grow, when you take on bigger contracts, or when customers expect to deal with a company. It also separates business and personal finances more cleanly.

It comes with formal duties. Directors have legal responsibilities. The company must file accounts and a confirmation statement with Companies House and deal with Corporation Tax with HMRC. Since 18 November 2025, identity verification has been a legal requirement for directors, and new companies need a verified personal code for each director when they register.

A company also needs a registered office address. If you rent a unit, ask your landlord before using the unit as your registered office. At The Rock Factory, ask us on WhatsApp and we will talk it through.

The company's bank account, contracts and invoices should all be in the company's name, not yours. Mixing personal and company money causes problems with tax and can weaken the protection that limited liability gives.

People often choose a limited company because they have heard it saves tax. Sometimes it does, sometimes it does not, and the answer depends on your profits, how you take money out, your other income and the rates for the year. That is a calculation for an accountant, not a rule of thumb.

VAT works the same way for both structures. You must register once your taxable turnover goes over the VAT threshold. For 2026/27, GOV.UK guidance puts the threshold at £90,000 of taxable turnover over a rolling 12 months, unchanged since April 2024. Check the current figure before relying on it.

Keep your own records clear whatever you choose. Good records make any accountant's advice cheaper, faster and more reliable.

1. Start with the riskIf your work could lead to large claims or debts, limited liability carries more weight.
  2. Look at your likely profitSmall or uncertain profits often favour the simplicity of being a sole trader.
  3. Consider your customersSome trade customers or contracts prefer working with a company.
  4. Weigh up the adminBe honest about how much paperwork you will keep on top of.
  5. Ask an accountantTake your rough figures and get a view based on the current tax year.

Many people start as a sole trader and incorporate later once things are established. Either way, our guide to starting a business in Blackpool covers the next steps.

If you are still unsure, a short paid session with an accountant is usually money well spent. Bring a rough forecast of your first year's sales and costs, and a list of the questions in this guide.

• "You need a company to look professional." Customers care more about good work, clear prices and reviews than about letters after your name.
  • "Sole traders cannot use a business name." They can, within the naming rules on GOV.UK.
  • "A company always pays less tax." It depends on profit levels and how you take money out. Get advice with real numbers.
  • "Limited liability protects you from everything." Personal guarantees on loans or leases, and some director duties, can still reach you personally.
  • "Setting up a company is a big job." Registering is fairly quick online. It is the ongoing filings that take the effort.

Whichever route you choose, keep business money separate, keep good records and diarise your deadlines. Those habits matter more than the structure itself.

This is general information, not legal, tax or accounting advice. Tax rates, allowances and Companies House requirements change, and the right structure depends on your personal circumstances. Check the GOV.UK and Companies House guidance below and speak to a qualified accountant before deciding.

faqs: Can I switch from sole trader to limited company later?
Yes. Many businesses start as sole traders and incorporate later. There are tax and admin steps involved, so it is worth planning the timing with an accountant.
Do I need an accountant to be a sole trader?
Not legally. Many sole traders do their own Self Assessment. An accountant can still save time and help you claim the right expenses.
Does a limited company protect my house?
Limited liability generally means the company's debts are the company's, but there are exceptions, such as personal guarantees or wrongful trading. Take advice if this is a concern.
Can I use my unit address as my registered office?
Ask your landlord first. At The Rock Factory, tenants can receive mail at their unit, but talk to us on WhatsApp before naming it as a registered office.
Do sole traders and companies have different VAT rules?
The VAT registration threshold applies to both. Once your taxable turnover passes it, you must register, whatever your structure.
Do I have to register a business name?

Sole traders do not register a name with Companies House, but GOV.UK sets out naming rules, such as not using sensitive words without permission. Limited company names are registered at Companies House when the company is formed.
