pages.title: Selling at Blackpool Markets | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: How to start selling at markets and events in Blackpool: finding pitches, licences from the council, food rules, stall kit and storing market stock.
h1: and storing your stall between events
pages.lead: Markets and events are one of the best ways to test a product, meet customers face to face and build a following. Here is how market trading works in Blackpool, what the council licenses, and how to keep your stall kit and stock organised.

sections.h2: Why markets work for small businesses
sections.html:
A market stall gives you instant feedback. You see which products people pick up, hear what they ask, and learn which prices make them hesitate. That is hard to get from an online shop alone.

Markets also build trust. People who have met you are more likely to follow you online, order again and recommend you. Many successful small brands started on a trestle table.

Start small. A few local fairs are a low-cost way to find out whether your product, prices and display work before you commit to a regular pitch or a permanent stall. Note the cost of each pitch against your takings, so you can compare events fairly.

sections.h2: Where to sell in and around Blackpool
sections.html:
Opportunities come in a few broad forms: permanent indoor markets with units or stalls, regular outdoor or themed markets, craft and makers' fairs, and one-off community or seasonal events.

In the town centre, Abingdon Street Market reopened after a council-funded refurbishment, with a food hall and retail units for independent traders. Blackpool Council has announced an operator to run it, so ask the market's operator directly about current opportunities, availability and terms.

Beyond that, look out for craft fairs, school and community events, and seasonal markets across the Fylde coast. Event listings, local social media groups and other traders are the best way to find out what is running and how to apply. Organisers' requirements vary, so always ask what they need from you.

Who you need permission from depends on where you sell.

  • Organised markets and fairs: the organiser or operator gives you a pitch and sets the rules. Ask whether they need to see insurance or other documents.
  • Streets and public land: Blackpool Council controls street trading. Its licensing pages explain that some streets are prohibited and others need consent, and that traders should not set up where they would cause an obstruction.
  • Private land: the council's guidance says you need the landowner's permission and should check that planning has no objections.
  • Pedlars: selling on foot from place to place is different, and needs a pedlar's certificate from the police.

Check the council's street trading and licensing pages, or contact its licensing team, before trading anywhere that is not an organised event.

If you sell food, the Food Standards Agency says you must register your food business with the local council, and it advises doing so at least 28 days before you start trading. Food safety training and labelling rules may apply too.

Many organisers ask for public liability insurance. If you make or sell products, product liability is worth considering, and you will want cover for stock and kit while it is in transit and at events. Our small business insurance guide explains the options.

Your takings are business income. Keep a simple record of sales and costs for each event, and register with HMRC when you need to.

A good kit makes setting up quick and selling easy. Keep it light, tough and packed in the same order every time.

  • Folding table, tablecloth and a gazebo with weights for outdoor events.
  • Risers, crates and baskets to give your display height.
  • Clear price labels and a simple sign with your name.
  • Card reader, float, notebook and a charged power bank.
  • Bags, wrapping and business cards.
  • A small toolkit: tape, clips, cable ties and scissors.

Think about how your stall looks from three metres away, where most shoppers decide whether to stop. One clear sign, a tidy display with some height and a few well-lit hero products usually work better than covering every inch of the table.

Market traders often run out of space at home long before they run out of customers. Gazebos, tables, display stands and boxes of stock take up a lot of room, and loading the car from an upstairs flat gets old quickly.

A ground-floor unit with a roller shutter lets you pack the car or van straight from the shelves. Our 150 sq ft roller-shutter unit at £65 a week suits a compact stall setup, and the 180 sq ft unit at £78 a week gives you room to prepare stock too. With 24-hour access, you can load up before an early start and drop everything back after a late finish.

  1. Zone your shelvesKeep event kit by the door and stock behind it, sorted by product.
  2. Pack event boxesPrepare a box per event the day before, ready to lift straight out.
  3. Check kit after each eventDry gazebos fully before storing and repair anything damaged straight away.

Dry goods, fabric, card and wooden display kit are all fine to store. Cooking and hot food are not allowed in our units, and bulk fuel or gas cylinders need our written agreement. See the unit ideas for market traders page for more ideas.

Your first event is as much about learning as selling. Go in with modest stock and an open mind.

  1. Arrive earlyGive yourself time to unload, set up and calm down before customers appear.
  2. Stand, do not sitStand beside your table, say hello and let people browse without pressure.
  3. Count what sellsTally each sale and note the questions people ask. It guides your next batch.
  4. Collect contactsOffer a card or a way to follow you online, so a browser can become a buyer later.
  5. Review that eveningNote the takings, costs and what you would change, while it is fresh.

Do not judge a market on one day. Weather, other events and the time of year all affect footfall. Try a few dates before deciding whether a market is worth your time.

This is general information, not legal or licensing advice. Market operators, events and council rules change. Check with the organiser and Blackpool Council's licensing pages before you trade, and with the Food Standards Agency if you sell food.

faqs: Do I need a licence to sell at a craft fair?
At an organised fair, the organiser usually handles the pitch. Ask what they require, such as insurance. Trading on streets or public land is controlled by Blackpool Council.
Can I sell food at markets?
Yes, with the right steps. The Food Standards Agency says food businesses must register with their local council, ideally at least 28 days before trading.
Can I store my market stall in a Rock Factory unit?
Yes. Tables, gazebos, display kit and dry stock are fine. Roller-shutter units make loading easier. Cooking, hot food, and bulk fuel or gas cylinders without written agreement are not allowed.
How do I find out about markets in Blackpool?
Ask the operators of indoor markets like Abingdon Street Market directly, follow local event listings and community groups, and talk to other traders, who often know about upcoming events first.
Do I need a card reader for market stalls?
It is not required, but many shoppers expect to pay by card. A portable reader and a small cash float cover most situations. Check signal at the venue beforehand, as some indoor spots are patchy.

pages.title: Running a Seasonal Business in Blackpool | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: How to run a seasonal business in Blackpool: planning around the visitor season and Illuminations, cash flow for winter and flexible storage.
pages.lead: Blackpool's visitor economy brings busy months and quiet ones. Whether you sell to tourists or to the businesses that serve them, planning for the swing is what keeps a seasonal business healthy.

sections.h2: The shape of the Blackpool year
sections.html:
Blackpool has been a holiday resort for generations, and its year still follows the visitors. Spring brings the first rush around the Easter holidays. Summer is the peak. Then the Illuminations switch on at the end of the summer and stretch the season well into the autumn, with festive events extending the lights season further in recent years.

After that, the town gets quieter, and many visitor-facing businesses scale down. Every business feels this differently. Some trades get busier in winter, for example decorators, repairers and businesses that refit hotels and holiday lets between seasons.

Dates change every year, so check Visit Blackpool for the current Illuminations season rather than relying on last year's.

The pattern also varies within each week. Weekends and school holidays are busier than midweek, and the weather can change a day completely. Many seasonal businesses track takings by day as well as by month, so they can plan staffing and stock more precisely.

You do not have to sell rock on the Promenade to be seasonal. Look at your sales over a year, or estimate them if you are new.

  • Visitor-facing: souvenirs, attractions, entertainment, photography, mobile catering run from separate premises.
  • Supplying the visitor trade: cleaning, linen, laundry, maintenance and printing for hotels and venues.
  • Event-led: hire businesses, decorators and entertainers working around weekends and holidays.
  • Weather-led: gardening, landscaping and outdoor services.
  • Gift-led: makers and online sellers who peak before Christmas.

Knowing your own pattern lets you plan stock, staff and cash around it.

sections.h2: Plan cash flow for the quiet months
sections.html:
The most common seasonal mistake is spending peak-season income as if it will keep coming. A simple plan avoids it.

  1. Map your monthsEstimate income and costs for each month of the year, not just the total.
  2. Set aside a winter fundMove a share of busy-month takings into a separate pot for the lean months.
  3. Put tax aside tooYour tax bill reflects the whole year, including the good months.
  4. Cut flexible costs off-seasonReduce stock, hours and space you do not need in winter.
  5. Plan winter workUse quiet months for maintenance, making stock, training and marketing.

Talk to your bank or accountant before the quiet months, not during them. It is easier to arrange support while your figures look strong.

sections.h2: Flexible space for a seasonal business
sections.html:
Your space needs change across the year as much as your income. In spring you might need room to build up stock. In summer you need quick access to restock. In winter you may only need somewhere dry to keep equipment and displays.

That is where rolling terms help. At The Rock Factory, there is a one-month minimum, then one month's notice, and you can swap to a bigger or smaller unit any time, subject to availability. Some units have interconnecting doors if you need to add space next door during a busy spell.

For off-season storage only, our seasonal storage guide covers packing and storing kit between seasons. First-floor storage pods are also planned for spring 2027 at guide prices, for smaller amounts.

If you want to scale down for winter or add space for the build-up, ask us on WhatsApp in good time so we can check what is free.

sections.h2: Making the most of the peak
sections.html:
Preparation in the quiet months pays off when the town is busy. Have stock made or bought, kit checked and staff lined up before the rush, not during it.

  • Keep your Google Business Profile hours accurate, including seasonal changes.
  • Restock during quieter hours, using 24-hour access if you have it.
  • Track what sells each week, so next year's buying is based on facts.
  • Ask peak-season customers to follow you online so you can reach them off-season.

If you take on seasonal staff, employer duties apply from the start, even for a short summer contract. GOV.UK says employers' liability insurance is compulsory once you employ people, and you will need to run payroll and check right to work. Health and safety duties apply too.

If you sell at events or markets in the season, check licensing and food rules in good time. Our guide to selling at Blackpool markets explains what the council controls.

The quiet months are not wasted time. Many seasonal businesses do their most important work when the Promenade is empty.

  • Build stock for next season at a steady pace, rather than in a panic in spring.
  • Repair, repaint and service equipment while it is not in use.
  • Review the year's sales and drop the lines that did not earn their space.
  • Update your website, photos and Google Business Profile.
  • Try a winter income stream, such as online sales, gifts, or work for local businesses.
  • Book any training or certificates you need before the rush.

Some businesses find a second season. Makers sell at Christmas markets, event businesses take on festive parties, and maintenance trades are busy getting hotels and holiday lets ready for spring. Looking for that winter demand can turn a three-month business into a year-round one.

sections.h2: A storage plan for the year
sections.html:
Think about your space in three phases.

PhaseWhat you needSpace tip
Build-upRoom to make or receive stockKeep a clear work area near the door
PeakFast restockingPut best sellers at the front, slow lines at the back
Off-seasonDry storage for kit and displaysClean, dry and label everything before it goes away

This is general information, not legal, tax or employment advice. Event dates change each year, and employment and tax rules depend on your circumstances. Check Visit Blackpool for event dates and GOV.UK for employer and tax rules, and speak to an accountant about cash flow and tax planning.

faqs: When is Blackpool's busy season?
Broadly from spring through the summer, with the Illuminations extending it into the autumn. Exact event dates change each year, so check Visit Blackpool.
Can I rent a unit just for the season?
Our terms are rolling monthly with a one-month minimum and one month's notice, so you can rent for as long as you need, subject to availability.
Do I need insurance for a summer helper?
If you employ them, GOV.UK says employers' liability insurance is compulsory from the start, with limited exemptions. Check the GOV.UK guidance before they begin.
Can I store seasonal stock in the same unit I work from?
Yes, as long as it is a permitted item. Dry goods, displays, fabric and wooden kit are fine, while bulk flammable liquids and gas cylinders need our written agreement.
Is the Illuminations season good for all businesses?

Not necessarily. It brings visitors to the Promenade, especially in the evenings, which helps some trades much more than others. Look at your own sales from previous years rather than assuming it will be your busiest time.
Should I close completely in winter?

Some businesses do, but many find steady winter work, such as online sales, Christmas markets or work for local hotels and venues preparing for the next season. Even a little off-season income eases the strain on cash flow.
